anatomy.intro: The ribs and the grass-blade-like spines are separate structures with very different shapes.

parts.function: Thin, strongly folded ribs divide the round green body.
parts.label: Wavy rib

parts.function: A small pale growing cushion occurs at intervals along a rib.
parts.label: Areole

parts.function: The long upper spine is broad and blade-like rather than a leaf.
parts.label: Flattened central spine

parts.function: Much shorter pale spines spread around the areole beneath the prominent central spine.
parts.label: Short radial spines

flowers.text: The usual species description gives small yellowish-white flowers with a reddish-brown throat. Pink- or violet-striped plants sold under this name can involve other forms or species, making a clear future flower photograph especially useful.

growth.note: Spine and flower characters should be considered together; a species label is stronger evidence than a common name, but it is still not proof.

stages.text: A young plant develops crowded ribs and its first contrasting spine groups.
stages.title: Compact globe

stages.text: Long flattened upper spines become conspicuous above the wavy body.
stages.title: Blade-spined adult

stages.text: The body can become somewhat taller and develop corky tissue near its base.
stages.title: Older plant

habitat.text: Kew records this species from Mexico in desert and dry shrubland. The profile’s nursery label is retained, but Stenocactus identification is not settled by a wavy outline alone: specialist descriptions emphasize variation and uncertain boundaries among closely related forms. Its unusual combination of narrow ribs and broad central spines is more useful than a single rib count.

lookalikes.name: Giant chin cactus
lookalikes.text: Gymnocalycium saglionis has broad, rounded tubercles and stout curved spines. Stenocactus has many thin wavy ribs with conspicuously flattened upper spines; both are ribbed globes, but their surface architecture differs.

mature.text: Specialist descriptions give bodies around 3–15 cm tall and 4–10 cm wide, usually solitary. Rib counts vary considerably; a compact pot specimen is not expected to match every published extreme.

milestones.text: Joined the collection from Costa Farms.
milestones.title: Acquired

nameStory.text: The accepted Stenocactus combination was published in 1929. Kew’s synonym list preserves older Echinocactus and Echinofossulocactus names, which explains why the same labeled plant can appear under unfamiliar headings in older books.
